lines.say: Here are four sealed boxes, and just one of them hides a prize.
A helper won't say which box it is, but will quietly mark it.
With Grover search, one look is enough. Here's how.
Each box gets an amplitude, a number whose square is its chance of showing up.
An H gate on each qubit makes it fair: every box gets one half, a one in four chance.
The helper, called the oracle, flips the prize box's sign, to minus one half.
But squaring it still gives one quarter, so the odds haven't changed.
Next, the diffuser reflects every amplitude around their average, which is now one quarter.
The other three sit a quarter above it, so they flip down to zero.
The prize sits three quarters below, so it's flung three quarters above, up to one.
Now one look finds it every time. That's interference, growing the prize and cancelling the rest.
With more boxes, one round isn't enough. It's like pushing a swing.
Each round, like a well timed push, lifts the prize a little higher.
For N boxes, the sweet spot is just under the square root of N rounds. Push longer and it swings back.
But a swing gains energy, and this never does. The chances always add up to one.
The prize only gains because every other box loses.
And it never opens every box at once. It reshapes amplitudes so one look is likely right.
So mark the answer with a sign, reflect around the average, and repeat about pi over four times root N.
